title: Intro to Political Science

jokes.text: Britta: 'I wanna go to rehab and compare penises with famous people.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has just told a crude celebrity bathroom story; the group reacts with 'Wow'
jokes.punchline: Britta earnestly declares this as a bucket-list item, treating something absurd as aspirational
jokes.explanation: Economical and funny — Britta's line is perfectly calibrated to her character (earnest, slightly unhinged feminist who would genuinely find this aspirational). The delivery of something inappropriate as sincere desire is a Britta specialty. Good but not exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: So Tom says to me, 'Size matters,' right?

dialogue.speaker: Tom
dialogue.line: Size matters.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: And I tell him: 'Size more? Try size less.'

jokes.text: Jeff: 'All in good time, kiddo.' — responding to Britta's rehab/penis wish with the tone of a patient mentor
jokes.setup: Britta has expressed a desire to compare penises with celebrities in rehab
jokes.punchline: Jeff responds as though this is a reasonable goal he's encouraging her toward, with paternal condescension
jokes.explanation: Four words doing a lot of work — Jeff's smug condescension applied to something utterly ridiculous is perfectly on-brand. Very economical. The 'kiddo' is the key word that makes it land. Functional rather than brilliant.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Pierce, why would you tell us that story?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: He's like a celebrity in rehab who doesn't understand why he's there.

jokes.text: The Dean bursting into the study room to announce Biden's visit — the group's immediate, ecstatic relief at any excuse not to study
jokes.setup: The group has reluctantly opened their Anthropology textbook to Chapter Four after Pierce's return
jokes.punchline: The Dean arrives and everyone immediately erupts: 'Oh, thank God! Yes! Oh, my God. Thank you.' — pure, unfiltered relief
jokes.explanation: The joke is in the collective reaction — these are people who attend school but have zero desire to actually do schoolwork. The timing of the Dean's arrival (literally the moment a textbook is opened) is a well-worn sitcom beat, but it's executed cleanly and the effusiveness of their gratitude is funny.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is torture. When are we ever going to use anthropology?

dialogue.speaker: Britta
dialogue.line: Understanding human culture is actually pretty important.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Can we please just be done with this?

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Study group! I need you all in my office immediately!

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's the most beautiful thing I've ever heard.

jokes.text: The Dean announces: Biden's 'Biden Time Talkin' 'Bout Teachin'' tour
jokes.setup: The Dean announces VP Biden is touring community colleges
jokes.punchline: The official name of the tour is a triple-layered Biden pun: 'Biden Time' (biding time) + 'Talkin' 'Bout Teachin'' (folksy alliterative framing)
jokes.explanation: Smart, dense wordplay that rewards attention. 'Biden Time' is a solid pun, but piling on 'Talkin' 'Bout Teachin'' signals that someone in the writers' room was having fun engineering the most Biden-ish tour name possible. Britta's follow-up ('Folksy, yet progressive') compounds the joke perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen, I'm pleased to announce that Vice President Joe Biden will be visiting Greendale Community College as part of his nationwide tour, which he's calling 'The Biden Identity.'

jokes.text: Britta: 'Mm, folksy, yet progressive. He does walk that line.'
jokes.setup: The Dean has named Biden's tour with its deliberately folksy title
jokes.punchline: Britta analyzes it with the gravity of a political scientist, as though 'walking the line between folksy and progressive' is a profound observation
jokes.explanation: Britta's pseudo-intellectual political analysis of a pun title is very on-brand. The joke is that she's treating a goofy tour name as if it reveals something deep about Biden's political positioning. Economical and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: The 'Build Back Better' tour? More like 'Build Back Bitter' — because that's what happens when you've been in politics longer than democracy's been on Netflix.

jokes.text: Dean: 'Eat that, City College, and wash it down with a nice tall glass of suck it.'
jokes.setup: Dean announces the VP is coming to Greendale — a point of institutional pride
jokes.punchline: His trash-talk escalates from 'eat that' to 'wash it down with a nice tall glass of suck it' — unexpectedly elaborate and aggressive from an academic administrator
jokes.explanation: The Dean's pathological rivalry with City College is a running character trait, and this line is a great expression of it. The escalation from 'eat that' to the more elaborate 'wash it down with a nice tall glass of suck it' is what makes it funny — the specificity of 'tall glass' is unexpected. Very quotable and character-specific.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Oh my God, a Biden visit! This is huge for Greendale!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We need to make sure our campus looks absolutely perfect. I'm thinking red carpet, maybe some bunting...

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Actually, you know what? Suck it, other schools!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Biden's coming HERE. To Greendale. Our Greendale!

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: SUCK IT!

jokes.text: Abed: 'That explains the people I've noticed covertly surveilling the campus this week. Must be Secret Service.'
jokes.setup: The Dean announces the VP is coming; everyone is surprised
jokes.punchline: Abed has apparently been watching Secret Service agents all week and simply categorized it as background information — his hyper-observant detachment is played completely straight
jokes.explanation: Classic Abed — he noticed something the entire Secret Service apparatus was trying to hide, treated it as unremarkable, and filed it away. The joke works because it's entirely consistent with who Abed is as a character: an observer who catalogues reality without emotional investment. The rewatch bonus is for how it seeds the Abed/Vohlers subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're being watched by the Secret Service.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Abed, the only thing you're being surveilled by is the Nielsen ratings.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Oh, Abed, will your reality ever come out on Blu-Ray so we can enjoy it?'
jokes.setup: Abed has casually mentioned noticing Secret Service surveillance all week
jokes.punchline: Jeff frames Abed's perception of reality as a media product — implying Abed experiences life like a movie and the rest of them are locked out of that version
jokes.explanation: One of the smarter Jeff lines in the episode — it manages to affectionately mock Abed's media-filtered worldview while itself being a media reference. It's the kind of meta-joke that Community specializes in: the character IS the joke type. Character-specific and witty, though not quite exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've been tracking the secret surveillance all week.

jokes.text: Abed: 'We've been made.' — responding to Jeff's Blu-Ray line by treating it as a spy-film moment
jokes.setup: Jeff has just joked about Abed's reality being like a Blu-Ray
jokes.punchline: Abed immediately switches into thriller-film mode, treating Jeff's comedic observation as a plot development — 'We've been made' implies they were undercover
jokes.explanation: Two words doing remarkable work. Abed re-genres the entire conversation — not as a community college meeting but as a spy scenario — and 'We've been made' is the perfect film-language signifier. The economy is flawless, the character integration is about as high as it gets for Abed. It's also a preview of the Abed/Secret Service subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: In espionage, we call that a 'burn notice.' You've been made.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton considering borrowing his sister's Uncle Sam outfit — 'It's tailored for ladies, but what else can I do on such short notice?'
jokes.setup: The Dean is panicking about what to wear for Biden's visit and mentions he could borrow his sister's Uncle Sam costume
jokes.punchline: He adds 'it's tailored for ladies' — implying he's seriously considered wearing a women's patriotic costume and his only objection is timing, not gender
jokes.explanation: Perfectly in-character for Dean Pelton, whose flamboyant costuming is a running element. The joke has two layers: the absurdity of the costume itself, and his resigned acceptance that 'tailored for ladies' is a minor inconvenience rather than a dealbreaker. His follow-up about not having a sister is the nail in the coffin.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: What should I wear to meet Biden? I want to make a good impression.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: You know what? I'll just wear my sister's feminine Uncle Sam outfit. The sequins really bring out my eyes.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Well, you can not dress up like Uncle Sam. Or admit you don't have a sister.'
jokes.setup: Dean says he may have to borrow his 'sister's' Uncle Sam costume
jokes.punchline: Jeff suggests two options: don't wear it, OR admit the sister doesn't exist — implying the Dean invented a sister to justify already owning a ladies' Uncle Sam outfit
jokes.explanation: Sharp and efficient. Jeff reads through the Dean's cover story instantly and lays out both the obvious solution and its implication — that the Dean already owns the outfit and fabricated the sister. The structure is clean: option A (normal), option B (devastating revelation). Rewatch bonus because the Dean will show up in the outfit anyway.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, Dean has a sister? Since when?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm pretty sure you just made that up right now.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Improving Greendale takes more than ideas, Annie. It takes time, gasoline, matches.'
jokes.setup: Annie says she has ideas for improving the school
jokes.punchline: Jeff's list of requirements escalates from reasonable ('time') to arson ('gasoline, matches') — implying the only real improvement would be burning it down
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'time' (expected) to 'gasoline, matches' (arson) is a perfect dark subversion. Jeff's nihilism about Greendale is completely in character, and the list structure builds and pays off efficiently. 'Mm, nice' as the response from another character confirms the room's reaction. Well-crafted.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We need to improve the school. I have some ideas for renovations and better programs.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Or we could just burn it down.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Well, news flash, Jeff. Some of us care about more than just fixing our hair and sculpting our abs.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is being dismissive of Annie's political aspirations
jokes.punchline: Annie skewers Jeff's vanity by naming his actual priorities — hair and abs — which is both an insult and completely accurate
jokes.explanation: Competent character-based jab that works because it's accurate. 'Hair and abs' is specific enough to land. Jeff's response ('Wow. You got me pegged.') is the funnier beat — his complete inability to be wounded by accurate insults is very Jeff.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You know what, Jeff? Your problem isn't that you're a cynic. Your problem is that you're vain. You'd rather be right about how terrible everything is than actually try to make things better.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not fair.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Isn't it? You spend more time on your hair than you do on your actual character, and we both know it.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Wow. You got me pegged.' — delivered without a trace of defensiveness
jokes.setup: Annie accuses Jeff of only caring about his hair and abs
jokes.punchline: Jeff fully agrees with zero shame — 'You got me pegged' — turning what was meant to be a wounding accusation into a compliment he accepts graciously
jokes.explanation: Four words that reveal everything about Jeff's character — he is completely unbothered by accurate assessments of his shallowness because he doesn't see them as flaws. The deflation of Annie's attempted insult is funnier than the insult itself. Perfect economy.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Oh, I'm sorry, is my intelligence and exceptional good looks making you feel insecure?

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Democracy. What a ruse. There's no such thing as a system in which the masses hold any...' / Everyone: 'Everyone wants you to shut up.' / Pierce: 'And yet I won't. Case in point.'
jokes.setup: Pierce begins a pompous anti-democracy speech
jokes.punchline: He's interrupted mid-sentence by a collective 'Everyone wants you to shut up,' which he immediately weaponizes as proof of his point about mass suppression — 'And yet I won't. Case in point.'
jokes.explanation: Smart piece of comedy architecture. Pierce's interruption by the group is a standard sitcom beat, but his pivot — turning the interruption into evidence supporting his interrupted argument — is clever and very Pierce. 'Case in point' lands hard because it's simultaneously self-unaware and technically correct. The structure of setup → interruption → reframing is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I know everyone hates when I talk, but I'm going to keep doing it anyway because that's what democracy is all about.

jokes.text: Dean Pelton presiding over the applause-based primary while actually wearing the ladies' Uncle Sam outfit — 'And yes, this is a ladies Uncle Sam outfit. It's my sister's. It was last-minute. I had no choice.'
jokes.setup: Jeff told the Dean earlier he could 'not wear' the costume or admit he has no sister
jokes.punchline: The Dean is wearing the costume anyway and defensively explaining the sister, completely validating Jeff's prediction
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff on Jeff's earlier observation. The Dean chose option C: wear the costume AND insist the sister is real. His desperate, unprompted explanation ('It was last-minute. I had no choice.') to an audience that hasn't asked is exactly right for the character. The visual of the Dean in a women's Uncle Sam costume presiding over a democratic primary is peak Community absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Before you say anything, this is a very patriotic outfit, and I will not apologize for my love of this country.

jokes.text: Secret Service agent Vohlers: 'I wonder if that's the same sister that tweets me to ask if I think her brother's cute.'
jokes.setup: Dean insists the costume belongs to his sister
jokes.punchline: Vohlers reveals the 'sister' has been tweeting her about the Dean — suggesting the Dean is using a fake account to fish for compliments from Secret Service agents
jokes.explanation: This is the best gag in the episode's first act. The reveal is unexpected, specific, and devastating — the Dean has been running a fake Twitter account pretending to be his sister in order to solicit compliments about himself from a Secret Service agent. It's funny on the first watch and funnier on rewatch. The deadpan delivery from a federal agent makes it land harder. Strong originality, tight structure, very quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dean, I've been following your sister on Twitter. Turns out she's got some very familiar tweet patterns. Same time zone, same IP address, same obsession with administrative minutiae.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: What are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Your sister is you, Dean. You've been catfishing the entire school as your own sibling.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: That's ridiculous!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Really? Because I just tweeted screenshots to everyone. You might want to log out of that account.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I'm sorry, Annie. I'm not the worker bee type. I'm more of a silverback gorilla with the claws of a lion, the teeth of a shark, and the quiet dignity of a tortoise.'
jokes.setup: Annie complains Jeff didn't hang her fliers properly
jokes.punchline: Jeff's self-description as a hybrid apex predator animal — culminating absurdly in 'the quiet dignity of a tortoise'
jokes.explanation: Jeff's narcissism expressed through a ridiculous animal-hybrid metaphor is very strong. The escalation — gorilla (powerful), lion claws (fierce), shark teeth (deadly) — lands with 'quiet dignity of a tortoise,' which is the perfect comic deflation. The tortoise is not a predator, not sexy, not what anyone expected, and yet Jeff delivers it with complete sincerity. Good quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh wow, Jeff threw away my campaign flyers. How... inconsiderate of him.

jokes.text: Garrett entering the ice cream line because he wanted ice cream, not to run for president
jokes.setup: Dean asks Garrett why he wants to be president
jokes.punchline: 'I wanted ice cream, so I got in line...' — Garrett literally just wanted the ice cream that happened to be next to the signup line
jokes.explanation: Classic Greendale absurdism — the democratic process capturing someone who was just trying to get a snack. Garrett is a recurring background character defined by his haplessness, and this is a great expression of that. The Dean's nonplussed 'He wanted ice cream' and the crowd applauding anyway compounds the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Jeff, will you help me campaign?

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, I'm going to be honest with you. I'm going to run this campaign with the cunning of a fox, the strength of a bear, the speed of a cheetah, and the quiet dignity of a tortoise.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Face it, Annie. Politics are all about ego, popularity, and parlor tricks. Don't kid a lawyer. / Annie: 'Well, if I see one, I'll won't.'
jokes.setup: Jeff lectures Annie that politics are about ego and parlor tricks, signing off with 'Don't kid a lawyer'
jokes.punchline: Annie fires back: 'Well, if I see one, I won't' — implying Jeff is not actually a lawyer (he had his degree revoked)
jokes.explanation: One of the sharpest exchanges in the episode. Jeff uses 'Don't kid a lawyer' as a smug closer, and Annie pivots it instantly into a callback to Jeff's disbarment — 'if I see one, I won't.' It's fast, devastating, completely character-specific (only Annie would know and deploy this), and requires no explanation. The structure is textbook: setup the cliché, invert the assumption. Approaches the 8.0 anchor benchmark.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: Because I want to make decisions that affect hundreds of people. Wait, that's not what this is?

jokes.text: Secret Service agent Vohlers approaches Abed for a bag search, revealing she's been assigned to monitor him
jokes.setup: Abed is watching the primary spectacle
jokes.punchline: Two federal agents suddenly materialize to search him — the joke being that the Secret Service has identified Abed as a person worth monitoring, implying his behavior read as suspicious to trained professionals
jokes.explanation: The payoff to Abed's earlier observation — the watchers are now watching the watcher. It's a satisfying structural callback and sets up the episode's B-plot. Character-specific in that Abed's detached observation style apparently reads as threatening to federal agents.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, larger causes are great until you realize they're just an excuse for people to feel superior to each other.

jokes.text: Abed: 'I guess I noticed because I'm used to being the only observer.' / Vohlers: 'Well, we're not used to being noticed.' / Abed: 'That sounds a little sad.'
jokes.setup: Vohlers asks how Abed noticed Secret Service surveillance
jokes.punchline: Abed explains his observer identity; Vohlers reveals agents aren't used to being seen; Abed offers 'That sounds a little sad' — genuine empathy delivered with total affect-flatness
jokes.explanation: Beautiful character-driven exchange. Abed's self-identification as 'the only observer' is funny but also oddly poignant. The mirror quality — two people who observe without being seen — creates genuine chemistry. 'That sounds a little sad' is delivered as matter-of-fact analysis but carries real warmth. This is Community at its best: jokes that also do character work.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Don't kid a lawyer.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You're not a lawyer, Jeff. You got your degree from an online university that also sells hot tubs.

jokes.text: Vohlers: 'He's clean. Although I could issue a warning for this bootleg of The Last Airbender.' / Abed: 'Where were you a week ago?'
jokes.setup: Vohlers declares Abed's bag clear of threats
jokes.punchline: She notes a bootleg DVD but Abed's response — 'Where were you a week ago?' — implies he suffered through the theatrical release (the 2010 M. Night Shyamalan film, widely considered terrible) and wishes he'd been stopped
jokes.explanation: Smart, economical pop-culture joke with real wit. The implication is that Abed saw the theatrical release (infamous as one of 2010's worst films) and is bitterly wishing a federal agent had intervened to stop him. It doesn't explain the joke — it trusts the audience. Very Abed. The bootleg as a lesser-of-two-evils is an unexpected inversion.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I notice everything. I'm like a human DVR with trust issues.

jokes.text: Vohlers: 'You can keep it.' — giving Abed back his Last Airbender bootleg after implying it was substandard
jokes.setup: Vohlers has found the bootleg DVD and Abed has lamented missing the theatrical release
jokes.punchline: She hands it back — 'You can keep it' — which retroactively confirms the theatrical release was worse, since the bootleg quality isn't even worth confiscating
jokes.explanation: Extends the Last Airbender joke with admirable economy — three words that imply the federal government has better things to do than confiscate evidence of this particular crime. Works as a coda to the previous joke.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Vohlers
dialogue.line: You know, I've been trained to notice the smallest details. A twitch, a glance, the way someone breathes.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Vohlers
dialogue.line: But I have to admit... I didn't see this coming.

jokes.text: Annie's debate opening: a detailed, specific platform including black mold removal, catching 'the asscrack bandit,' and balancing the budget through 'administrative redundancies'
jokes.setup: Annie is asked what she'll do as president
jokes.punchline: Her platform is a mix of mundane school maintenance, a specific ongoing campus crime (the 'asscrack bandit'), and corporate jargon — the specificity of Greendale's particular dysfunction is the joke
jokes.explanation: The 'asscrack bandit' is a Greendale-specific running gag that makes this feel lived-in and specific to the world. Annie's earnestness in running on a platform of black mold and petty crime is a great character joke. The rewatch bonus is for 'asscrack bandit' fans who know the eventual Season 5 resolution.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Keenlan
dialogue.line: What is this? A screenplay for 'The Last Airbender'?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Yeah, I was working on a fan script—

dialogue.speaker: Agent Keenlan
dialogue.line: We need to go back further. Way further. Someone should have stopped this before it became a movie.

jokes.text: Troy's on-air name reveal: 'I'm Troy "Butt Soup" Barnes. What? That's my name.'
jokes.setup: Troy introduces himself as a co-anchor on campus TV, using a standard anchor format
jokes.punchline: 'Butt Soup' as his middle name — delivered with a defensive 'what?' as if anticipating the audience's reaction, then doubling down with 'that's my name'
jokes.explanation: Pure absurdist name comedy with an excellent defensive follow-up. 'What? That's my name' is the perfect button — Troy anticipates disbelief and preemptively argues against it, which makes it funnier. The specificity of 'Butt Soup' (not just gross, but conceptually incoherent as a name) elevates it. Highly quotable.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The Last Airbender movie is an insult to the source material and everyone involved should be ashamed.

jokes.text: Abed and Troy's candidate introductions: 'Garrett. That guy's just a mess. It's like God spilled a person.'
jokes.setup: Abed introduces each candidate with a brief profile
jokes.punchline: Garrett's bio ends with Troy's summary: 'It's like God spilled a person' — an abstract description of Garrett's hapless energy
jokes.explanation: Best pure joke in the episode. 'It's like God spilled a person' is an astonishingly original image for describing someone who seems accidental — as if they weren't made so much as dropped. It's maximally economical (six words), captures something true about Garrett's character, and is the kind of phrase you've never heard before but immediately understand. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor in originality and far exceeds it. This is the episode's closest to a truly exceptional joke.

dialogue.speaker: Student
dialogue.line: And that's why we need to abolish hierarchical structures and implement a direct democracy where every voice is equally heard.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Yeah, no one cares. You're not getting elected.

jokes.text: Abed introduces Leonard Rodriguez: 'Did he change his last name?' / 'Yeah, he's trying to court the Hispanic vote.'
jokes.setup: Leonard is introduced as 'Leonard Rodriguez'
jokes.punchline: The name is apparently new — Leonard has adopted a Hispanic surname to appeal to Hispanic voters, implying he (a visibly elderly white man) is committing election-year ethnic pandering
jokes.explanation: Smart political satire. The image of elderly Leonard changing his surname to court the Hispanic vote is a pointed parody of political identity pandering. It's also very specific to Leonard as a character — his self-serving, unselfconscious behavior makes this plausible within the show's world.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I believe in things that are good, and I'm against things that are bad. I think we should have more of what we want, and less of what we don't want. And I'm pretty sure that's what you want too.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Pierce Hawthorne. The wizard of wet wipes.' / Troy: 'I live with that dude. He's got night terrors and a rotary phone.'
jokes.setup: Pierce is introduced as a candidate
jokes.punchline: Troy, who lives with Pierce, provides personal intel: night terrors and a rotary phone — two details that together paint a perfect portrait of Pierce's archaic, anxious existence
jokes.explanation: Very economical character work. 'Night terrors and a rotary phone' is a perfect two-item list — one suggests psychological damage, one technological obsolescence. Together they capture Pierce's character (old, damaged, out of touch) with minimal words. The specificity of 'rotary phone' over just 'old phone' is the detail that makes it work.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: I'm Troy Barnes.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: My middle name is Barnes with an 'e'. My parents were very creative.

jokes.text: Abed: 'Magnitude. Short for Magnetic Attitude. He's a one-man party.'
jokes.setup: Magnitude is introduced as a candidate
jokes.punchline: His name is revealed to be a contraction of 'Magnetic Attitude' — an absurd but internally consistent logic for a person who is defined entirely by his social energy
jokes.explanation: Good character-building joke. 'Magnetic Attitude' as the full name is funny precisely because someone thought this was a name worth having. 'He's a one-man party' is a decent description but less novel. The setup is better than the punchline.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: This is Leonard, our student body president candidate.

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Actually, I've changed my name to something more relatable to the student body.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Oh yeah? What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Leonard
dialogue.line: Paco.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not pandering at all.

jokes.text: Annie confronts Jeff about not sincerely running: 'I will make you cry.' / Jeff: 'Mmm. Oh, I feel a slight ego blowing in from the east.' / Annie: 'You're gonna feel my foot blowing in from the south.'
jokes.setup: Annie tells Jeff she'll make him cry if he doesn't drop out
jokes.punchline: Jeff responds with a mock-meteorological metaphor ('ego blowing in from the east'); Annie pivots it into a physical threat ('foot blowing in from the south') — she extends his weather metaphor but escalates to violence
jokes.explanation: Good sparring dialogue with a nice structural move — Annie takes Jeff's metaphor and escalates it. The 'foot from the south' is funny because it maintains the meteorological framing while making a direct physical threat. Jeff and Annie's argumentative chemistry is well-served here.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Garrett is like a beautiful mistake. Like God was trying to make someone else and accidentally created him instead. He's what happens when the universe hiccups.

jokes.text: Annie confronts Jeff: 'You're not running sincerely.' Jeff: 'I know, and yet, the people love me. It's almost as if politics were a huge joke.'
jokes.setup: Annie accuses Jeff of running insincerely
jokes.punchline: Jeff agrees and treats the mass appeal of his insincere campaign as proof of a thesis about politics
jokes.explanation: Jeff's total lack of shame combined with turning the situation into a political theory is very him. 'It's almost as if politics were a huge joke' is delivered with false wonder. Functions well as satirical commentary.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: His name is Magnitude. It's short for 'Magnetic Attitude.'

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: That's not how abbreviations work.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Bring it on, Ponce de Leon.' / Jeff: 'I'm gonna, Greg Muldunna.' / Jeff: 'It's a real guy. He owns a mattress store downtown. You can look it up.'
jokes.setup: Annie and Jeff are trading trash-talk names
jokes.punchline: Jeff responds to 'Ponce de Leon' with 'Greg Muldunna' — a completely unknown person — then immediately defends its validity by offering verifiable references: a mattress store owner you can Google
jokes.explanation: Genuinely original comedy. The convention of trash-talk uses historical or fictional badasses as insults; Jeff subverts this with a hyperlocal, completely unmemorable real person. The fact that he verifies 'Greg Muldunna' exists — 'He owns a mattress store downtown. You can look it up.' — doubles down on the absurdity. The more mundane and specific the person, the funnier it gets. This is the kind of joke that only exists in a writer's room with real ambition.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Vohlers
dialogue.line: So what's your story? You seem like you've got some kind of subplot going on.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I do. And you're in one too.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Vohlers
dialogue.line: What? No, I'm not.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: You're a federal agent investigating a community college. That's definitely a subplot.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Vohlers
dialogue.line: I... suppose you're right.

jokes.text: Pierce threatening Vicki mid-debate, mic still on: 'I'm gonna eat your brains, Vicki. I'm gonna slurp 'em right out of that melon you call a head.'
jokes.setup: Pierce has been heckling Vicki; a reminder that the microphones are on is given
jokes.punchline: Pierce escalates to a graphic brain-eating threat with the specificity and relish of someone who has thought about this — 'slurp 'em right out of that melon'
jokes.explanation: Very Pierce. The horror of the image ('slurp 'em right out of that melon') is delivered with the casual specificity of someone who's rehearsed this threat. The word 'melon' is the detail that elevates it from generic threat to Pierceism. The microphone-is-on setup that he completely ignores compounds the joke.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: You know what? I was going to come back with something really cutting, but... I just can't. I'm too tired. It's like that guy from the mattress store commercial said: 'Your back'll thank you.'

jokes.text: Pierce: 'Well, they better be, 'cause I'm on fire up here.' — responding to the reminder that his microphone is on
jokes.setup: Pierce has been making threatening, unhinged statements; the moderator reminds him the mics are on
jokes.punchline: Pierce treats the mic reminder as a compliment — 'I'm on fire up here' — completely misreading the concern as validation of his performance
jokes.explanation: Good Pierce character comedy. His inability to process social feedback as negative — turning a warning into a compliment — is very consistent. 'I'm on fire up here' said with complete sincerity after threatening to eat someone's brain is a good ironic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You listen here, Vicki. I've forgotten more about intimidation than you'll ever know. I once made a man so scared, he aged thirty years in a single day. Now that man is dead. I did that. With words. And a look. This look. So you better watch yourself, because I will hurt you in ways that modern medicine hasn't even invented yet. I'll break bones that don't exist yet. I'll make you regret things you haven't even done. That's the kind of power I have.

jokes.text: Jeff's debate answer: name-dropping 'Jeremy' and 'Maria' as relatable constituents, then shuffling words: 'These people don't want me to say what I'll do. They want me to do what I'll say.'
jokes.setup: Jeff is asked what he'll do as president — a direct policy question
jokes.punchline: He responds with political-speech techniques (naming regular people, rhetorical chiasmus) and says literally nothing of substance. The chiasmus 'say what I'll do / do what I'll say' is the tell — it sounds profound but is meaningless
jokes.explanation: Sharp political satire. The chiasmus ('say what I'll do / do what I'll say') is a perfect parody of political doublespeak — it sounds like it means something but is a logical tautology. Troy's laugh-track observation 'Oh, they love it when you shuffle the words around' makes it explicit and funnier. This joke has real satirical teeth.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: Everyone heard you threaten her, Pierce.

jokes.text: Troy: 'Oh. They love it when you shuffle the words around.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has just delivered empty political rhetoric using chiasmus
jokes.punchline: Troy's instant, accurate deconstruction of political speech technique — 'shuffle the words around' — is both the funniest and most accurate description of that rhetorical device
jokes.explanation: Troy accidentally writes the best political science thesis in the room. 'Shuffle the words around' is funnier than any academic description of chiasmus, and it's the kind of guileless insight that is Troy's comedic specialty. The economy is excellent — six words that puncture an entire tradition of political rhetoric.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: We have a serious problem. There's someone going around campus deliberately exposing their butt crack to unsuspecting students.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: We're calling him the Ass Crack Bandit.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: This is not funny. We need to treat this as a serious threat to campus security.

jokes.text: Magnitude's entire debate answer: 'Pop! Pop!'
jokes.setup: Dean asks Magnitude what he'll do as president (same question as everyone else)
jokes.punchline: Magnitude's answer is 'Pop! Pop!' — his catchphrase — which is not an answer but which the crowd loves
jokes.explanation: Magnitude is a brilliantly conceived joke character — his entire personality is a catchphrase, 'Pop! Pop!', and the show's genius is in how it treats this as sufficient. As a political debate answer, 'Pop! Pop!' is simultaneously the worst possible response and, within the show's universe, entirely effective. The crowd goes wild. It's a perfect absurdist comment on political style over substance. Character integration and economy scores are as high as they can be — there is no other character who could do this, and two words say everything.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: My fellow students, I promise to bring change to Greendale. Together, we will achieve paradigm-shifting synergies through dynamic actualization of our collective potential.

jokes.text: Abed's interview with Vohlers about why he repeated first grade: 'I didn't know how to use scissors, I sat in the middle of the seesaw, and I always found the distinction between duck and goose to be very arbitrary.'
jokes.setup: Vohlers asks Abed a background-check question: why did he repeat first grade?
jokes.punchline: His three reasons reveal a child-Abed applying adult analytical frameworks to games: the seesaw middle as logical optimization, duck-duck-goose as arbitrary taxonomical distinction
jokes.explanation: One of the best jokes in the episode. Each of the three reasons reveals something true about Abed: he doesn't understand physical intuition (scissors), he applies game theory to playground equipment (seesaw — sitting in the middle DOES balance it equally), and he has a philosopher's objection to arbitrary categorization (duck vs. goose). The list builds beautifully. 'I always found the distinction between duck and goose to be very arbitrary' is not just funny — it's a perfect insight about the character, and it's genuinely philosophically interesting. Near-exceptional.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Dean, I'm going to use a lot of big words and shuffle them around to sound smart, but it won't actually mean anything.

dialogue.speaker: Dean
dialogue.line: Jeff, I went to a lot of seminars.

jokes.text: Vohlers: 'Couldn't you just pick the sixth kid every time?' / Abed: 'That's what I... Would have done.' / Vohlers: 'I went with four.'
jokes.setup: Abed has explained his objection to the duck/goose distinction
jokes.punchline: Vohlers and Abed discover they both developed systematic strategies for duck-duck-goose as children — bonding over shared childhood rule-gaming — 'I went with four'
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Vohlers also systematized duck-duck-goose is a perfect character pairing moment. 'I went with four' is said with the casual certainty of someone who worked this out long ago. It transforms a funny explanation about Abed into a meet-cute between two people who experience the world the same way. Economical, character-rich, and genuinely charming. This exchange is what makes the B-plot work.

dialogue.speaker: Magnitude
dialogue.line: Pop pop!

jokes.text: Troy (observing Abed and Vohlers bonding): 'Geez, get a room, you two.'
jokes.setup: Abed and Vohlers are having an oddly intimate exchange about childhood game theory
jokes.punchline: Troy recognizes it as a romantic connection and applies the standard phrase — accurately reading a situation that hasn't involved any physical contact or obvious flirtation
jokes.explanation: Functional reaction beat that earns a mild laugh. 'Get a room' is a cliché, but Troy's ability to read romantic subtext in a conversation about children's games is a decent gag. It's more of a punctuation beat than a crafted joke.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Vohlers
dialogue.line: You two need to get a room.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We're in the study room.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Vohlers
dialogue.line: I mean for your nerdy bonding.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'My platform will be one high enough to push Vicki off to her death.'
jokes.setup: Dean asks Pierce about his platform as a candidate
jokes.punchline: Pierce pivots the word 'platform' (political) to its literal meaning (raised surface) and uses it to announce he wants to murder Vicki — a minor candidate he's been heckling all episode
jokes.explanation: Exceptional wordplay with a dark twist. Pierce's wordplay on 'platform' is genuinely clever — taking a political metaphor literally to construct a murder threat is unexpected and very Pierce. The callback to his ongoing fixation on Vicki makes it funnier. The delivery would be completely deadpan. 'High enough to push Vicki off to her death' is a great line. Approaches the 8.0 anchor.

dialogue.speaker: Secret Service Agent
dialogue.line: Why did you repeat first grade?

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I had a logical reason. The other kids weren't ready for my level of discussion. I kept trying to talk to them about narrative structure and film theory, but they just wanted to play tag. So I figured I should wait a year for them to mature.

dialogue.speaker: Secret Service Agent
dialogue.line: That's not how school works.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: I'm aware now.

jokes.text: Vicki withdraws from the race; then another candidate immediately says 'Oh, well, then I am too. I was only here to get back at her for not lending me a pencil.'
jokes.setup: Pierce's murder threat causes Vicki to withdraw; another candidate also withdraws
jokes.punchline: The second withdrawal was motivated entirely by petty pencil vengeance — suggesting two people entered a democratic election over a pencil dispute
jokes.explanation: Classic Community background absurdism. The pencil-revenge motivation reduces democratic participation to its most petty possible form. It's also a setup for Pierce's final scene payoff (Vicki lending him the pencil). Good escalation joke that also plants a callback seed.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what? I'm dropping out. Vicki's right. This whole thing was a mistake.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Wait, what? Pierce, you were winning.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Winning? Jeff, my entire campaign was built on getting back at Vicki for stealing my pencil in the third grade.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'I don't, Annie. I think it's clean. I think it's the cleanest school in the entire country. You know it is.'
jokes.setup: Annie says everyone knows the school is dirty (with actual mold)
jokes.punchline: Jeff makes an objectively false statement with complete confidence — 'the cleanest school in the entire country' — delivered as though it's obvious and Annie is the crazy one
jokes.explanation: Extends the political satire — Jeff is now actively gaslighting the electorate about a known health hazard with total commitment. The specificity of 'the entire country' is a nice overclaim. It's good satire but functions more as an escalating scene beat than a standalone joke.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Well, I believe in a strong platform. You know, something you can really stand on.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Which is why I've been practicing my swing with this two-by-four.

jokes.text: Abed and Troy's campaign coverage: 'According to our polls, the campus is almost evenly divided. Now keep in mind the margin of error on this thing is about 98%.'
jokes.setup: Abed delivers poll results as a TV news anchor
jokes.punchline: 'Margin of error is about 98%' — which means the poll is functionally meaningless, followed by Troy's explanation that they asked two people at a vending machine
jokes.explanation: Solid media satire. '98% margin of error' is a good joke on its own, but 'Could be higher. We don't even know how to do margins of error. We talked to two people at a vending machine.' escalates it perfectly. The deadpan delivery of increasingly damning admissions about their methodology is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: My campaign slogan is 'A vote for Annie is a vote against the black mold!' It rhymes!

jokes.text: Annie's debate moment: 'No matter what you're told / We have to clean the mold.' — turning black mold removal into a chanting rhyming slogan
jokes.setup: Annie has been struggling to compete with Jeff's empty rhetoric and crowd-pleasing
jokes.punchline: She reduces her entire platform to a chanting rhyming couplet about mold — which the crowd actually responds to, suggesting the electorate responds to form over substance regardless of content
jokes.explanation: Smart political satire. Annie learns from Jeff's empty rhetoric and applies the formula to her substantive issue — the result is a genuinely catchy slogan about black mold. The irony is that Annie's real issue (the mold) becomes political currency only when it's turned into an empty chant. Good character arc joke.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Read my lips, no new hips!

jokes.text: Abed and Troy: 'Stay tuned.' / 'They have to stay tuned. It's closed circuit television.' / 'Don't know what that means.'
jokes.setup: Abed signs off with a standard broadcast 'stay tuned'
jokes.punchline: Troy correctly notes closed-circuit television means viewers have no choice but to watch, then admits he doesn't know what that means — the meta-commentary on their fake newscast undermines itself
jokes.explanation: Smart little exchange. The 'closed circuit' observation is legitimately correct and funny, but Troy immediately undermining himself with 'Don't know what that means' adds a second level. The structure — insight followed by self-negation — is clean and very Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: According to our poll, 73% of students prefer orange juice to apple juice, with a margin of error of 98%.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Which means the actual number could be anywhere from negative 25% to 171%.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So basically, our polling methodology is completely worthless.

jokes.text: Jeff at the debate break: 'Can I get an apple juice, please? Freshly squeezed this time or so help me God, Maurice.'
jokes.setup: During a debate break, Jeff addresses someone named Maurice
jokes.punchline: Jeff's entitled demand for 'freshly squeezed' apple juice — with a threat to God attached — implies he has both a named catering contact and deeply specific juice standards at a community college student debate
jokes.explanation: Good character joke — Jeff's demand for artisanal juice at a school debate reveals his reflexive need to treat every situation as though he's a VIP. 'So help me God, Maurice' is a funny name-drop of an unnamed character. It implies a previous incident where Maurice failed on the freshly-squeezed front.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Our polling methodology is completely scientific.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: We asked twelve people in the cafeteria.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: All of them were eating pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So our margin of error is plus or minus... pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: As for broadcast quality, we're using my laptop.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: The one with a cracked screen.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: And one dead pixel that looks like a tear.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: So every newscast looks like I'm emotionally devastated by the news.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Our camera work is handheld.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Because we don't have a tripod.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: So it's like watching the news during an earthquake.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: In a canoe.

jokes.text: Abed to Vohlers: 'Because you think I'm suspicious? Or because you wish I was suspicious, so that you would have an excuse to see more of me.'
jokes.setup: Vohlers claims the dorm search is a random spot check
jokes.punchline: Abed cuts through the pretense with movie-romance directness — not flirtatiously, but analytically, as though diagnosing her motivation
jokes.explanation: Very strong Abed moment. His romance-movie literacy allows him to skip all the subtext and go directly to the meta-analysis of the scene he's in — he's not flirting, he's diagnosing a plot beat. The line is simultaneously charming and clinical, which is exactly Abed's brand. 'An excuse to see more of me' would be arrogant from anyone else but reads as a neutral observation from him.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: I need fresh-squeezed apple juice. If it's not fresh-squeezed, I will hurt you.

jokes.text: Abed to Agent Vohlers: 'Because you think I'm suspicious? Or because you wish I was suspicious, so that you would have an excuse to see more of me.'
jokes.setup: Agent Vohlers explains the room search was a random spot check
jokes.punchline: Abed cuts through the official explanation with a romantic interpretation — suggesting she made up a pretext to spend time with him
jokes.explanation: Abed flirting is funny because it's Abed — his social literalism usually makes human connection difficult, so a confident romantic gambit delivered with this certainty is both surprising and charming. It also works as genre awareness: he's identified the romantic subplot structure and is playing his role.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Your interrogation technique is very... effective. Is that lavender soap?

dialogue.speaker: Agent Vohlers
dialogue.line: It's standard issue.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Well, it smells really good. I mean, not in a weird way. In a... professional way.

jokes.text: Vohlers: 'That's close enough.' / Abed: 'Are you sure?' / Vohlers: 'You smell like nice soap.' / Abed: 'I have to go.'
jokes.setup: Abed has correctly identified that Vohlers wants to see more of him
jokes.punchline: Vohlers blurts out 'You smell like nice soap' as an involuntary confession — having just been analyzed as having romantic intent, she immediately proves it by saying something awkwardly intimate. Abed's response ('I have to go') is the perfect deadpan retreat.
jokes.explanation: 'You smell like nice soap' is an oddly specific, completely awkward thing to say to someone you're supposed to be conducting a security check on. It's the kind of involuntary overshare that happens when social filters fail. Combined with Abed's immediate flat-affect retreat ('I have to go'), the exchange is both funny and genuinely charming. High quotability — it's a weirdly specific phrase that sticks.

dialogue.speaker: Agent Vohlers
dialogue.line: I'm going to miss you, Abed. You know, in another life, if you were just a little bit more of a criminal, this could have really gone somewhere.

jokes.text: Abed: 'I'm sorry you weren't a more obvious potential threat to the country.'
jokes.setup: Abed and Vohlers are having an awkward near-romantic moment during what was supposed to be a security check
jokes.punchline: Abed apologizes for failing to be a terrorist — a sincere expression of regret that she has no professional excuse to stay
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines in the episode, possibly the series. It's a romantic apology for not being a national security threat — a sentence that has essentially never been said in human history. The logic is perfect: Abed understands she needs a pretext, he doesn't have one, he's genuinely sorry about that. It's funny, oddly sweet, and delivers maximum meaning in minimum words. The character integration is essentially perfect — only Abed would think to say this, in exactly this way. Comfortably at the 8.0+ level.

dialogue.speaker: Starburns
dialogue.line: I'm withdrawing from the race. Politics would cut into my drug business.

jokes.text: Starburns: 'Yeah, I actually withdraw my candidacy. I fear a political career will shine a negative light on my drug dealing.'
jokes.setup: Starburns is asked about the black mold issue
jokes.punchline: He withdraws for the most honest possible reason — he's a drug dealer and doesn't want scrutiny — delivered as a straight career calculation
jokes.explanation: Very Greendale. Starburns's drug dealing is a background character trait and this line makes it explicit in the most casually honest way. 'Shine a negative light on my drug dealing' treats the drug trade as a legitimate career concern to be managed — the euphemism 'negative light' in this context is funny. Character-specific and economical.

dialogue.speaker: Starburns
dialogue.line: I'm withdrawing from the election campaign.

dialogue.speaker: Starburns
dialogue.line: I've realized I need to focus on what's really important - my methamphetamine lab.

jokes.text: Jeff: 'What's your favorite color? Mine's a three-way tie: red, white, and blue.'
jokes.setup: Jeff asks his opponents their 'favorite color' instead of a policy question, then answers his own question with patriotic colors
jokes.punchline: The question is an empty political gesture; Jeff's answer — a 'three-way tie' of the American flag colors — is perfect political pandering delivered with self-aware cynicism
jokes.explanation: Good political satire. The 'three-way tie: red, white, and blue' is a solid joke — the concept of a favorite color being a patriotic flag is transparently manipulative, and Jeff delivers it with knowing cynicism. 'Three-way tie' is the specific word choice that makes it land.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Blue. It's patriotic, it's sophisticated, it's the color of my eyes.

jokes.text: Dean: 'Magnitude, a response?' / Magnitude: 'I think you know, dean. Pop! Pop!'
jokes.setup: Jeff has asked candidates their favorite color using a patriotic answer
jokes.punchline: Magnitude's preface — 'I think you know, dean' — implies that 'Pop! Pop!' is so well-established that the Dean should have anticipated this response before even asking
jokes.explanation: The third iteration of the Magnitude running gag, and it's arguably the funniest. 'I think you know, dean' adds a new layer — Magnitude is now gently chiding the Dean for asking a question with an obvious answer. The catchphrase has become so established within the episode's internal logic that not knowing what's coming is the Dean's failure. Perfect running gag escalation.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: I have something to show you. It's an old audition tape of yours.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: Annie, no. Please don't.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Oh yes. I'm playing the nuclear option here.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You're going to watch yourself from ten years ago, and it's going to be embarrassing.

jokes.text: Annie produces Jeff's 1997 MTV Real World: Seattle audition tape as her 'audio-visual presentation'
jokes.setup: Annie announces she has an 'audio-visual presentation' for her debate closing statement — implying policy material
jokes.punchline: The presentation is a 1997 audition tape Jeff made for Real World: Seattle, complete with him singing a George Michael parody song about wanting to be on MTV
jokes.explanation: Major comedic setpiece. The misdirection (policy presentation → embarrassing personal video) is well-executed, and a 1997 Real World audition tape is a perfect choice for maximum Jeff humiliation. 19-year-old Jeff desperately wanting to be on reality TV is both funny and a believable character detail. The audience reaction and Jeff's 'What? What?' escalates it perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm gonna show you my potential, make it monumental, get you sentimental with my credentials.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm a sexy Christmas tree, come and decorate me, don't be afraid to be naughty and ornament me.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I'm a sexy Christmas tree!

jokes.text: Jeff: 'Oh, I set him up.' — Said admiringly after Magnitude's Pop Pop answer beats him
jokes.setup: Jeff designed the question to give himself an easy patriotic answer; Magnitude one-upped him with 'Pop! Pop!'
jokes.punchline: Jeff acknowledges his own defeat with admiration rather than anger — recognizing a superior political move
jokes.explanation: Good reaction beat. Jeff's sporting admiration for being out-maneuvered by a catchphrase humanizes him while satirizing political image-making.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: I was younger when I made that tape.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: You were 30.

jokes.text: Young Jeff on the audition tape singing a George Michael-esque song about applying to Real World: Seattle
jokes.setup: Annie plays the tape; we see/hear 19-year-old Jeff
jokes.punchline: Jeff is earnestly performing a pop ballad about wanting to be on MTV's Real World — the antithesis of his current cool, detached persona
jokes.explanation: The visual/audio of young Jeff earnestly singing for a reality show audition is one of the episode's big laugh moments. The specific choice of a George Michael-style ballad is perfect — aspirational, sincere, completely humiliating for the person he became. It's also a canonical character revelation: Jeff desperately wanted fame and validation, which tracks with everything we know about him.

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: This is a nightmare! My reputation is destroyed. Everything I've built is gone!

dialogue.speaker: Jeff
dialogue.line: And you know what? I hope Annie's student government campaign fails miserably. I hope nobody votes for her.

jokes.text: Annie: 'We've all been 19, Jeff, and none of us did this. None of us.' / Magnitude: 'Pop! Pop!' / Jeff: 'I hate you!'
jokes.setup: Jeff is mortified by the audition tape; Annie twists the knife
jokes.punchline: Magnitude's perfectly timed 'Pop! Pop!' after Annie's devastating line sends Jeff completely over the edge — 'I hate you!'
jokes.explanation: Perfect use of the running gag as an escalation tool. Magnitude's 'Pop! Pop!' at the worst possible moment for Jeff — after his most humiliating public moment — sends him into a full meltdown. The catchphrase was funny three times before; here it's the catalyst for a character breaking point. 'I hate you!' to Magnitude specifically is funnier than any other possible target.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, I've learned something in my years. Life's like a bottle of wine - it gets better with age, but sometimes it just turns into vinegar and you have to throw it out.

jokes.text: Jeff's full meltdown: 'I hate this school! And I hope you all get black mold poisoning!'
jokes.setup: Jeff has been humiliated by the Real World tape and pushed over the edge by Magnitude
jokes.punchline: Jeff's breakdown culminates in wishing black mold poisoning on the entire student body — ironically the very issue Annie was running to fix, now weaponized as a curse
jokes.explanation: Jeff's specific choice of 'black mold poisoning' as his curse is a great callback — it's the exact thing Annie has been campaigning about all episode. His breakdown accidentally confirms the black mold is real and the threat is legitimate. The escalation of 'I hate you! I hate this school!' to a specific environmental health curse is very funny.

dialogue.speaker: Annie
dialogue.line: Wow, Pierce, that's actually really wise.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know what? I've been waiting my whole life to say something smart. Turns out all I needed was to get the pencil I wanted.

jokes.text: Jeff in the bathroom: 'I've already established the men's room doesn't work.' — to Annie who's found him there to 'be alone'
jokes.setup: Jeff retreats to the men's room to be alone after his meltdown
jokes.punchline: Annie tracks him down there; Jeff's response implies he has previously attempted to use the men's room as a sanctuary and confirmed it doesn't function as one
jokes.explanation: Good economy. 'I've already established' implies prior attempts and observations — Jeff has been workshopping bathroom solitude and has empirical data that it fails. The phrasing is very Jeff: treating personal retreat as a research problem.

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about life, and I've realized that what really matters is—

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Wait, is that my pencil?

dialogue.speaker: Pierce
dialogue.line: Never mind, everything I just said is true.

jokes.text: Jeff's self-diagnosis: 'I am a gross, jaded adult with control issues that couldn't let a young, bright, idealistic kid run for president.'
jokes.setup: Jeff has been confronted by Annie about going too far with the Real World tape
jokes.punchline: Jeff delivers a perfectly accurate self-assessment with complete sincerity — 'gross, jaded adult with control issues' — the joke being that his self-awareness doesn't prevent his behavior
jokes.explanation: More character beat than crafted joke. Jeff's self-awareness is a running theme — he knows exactly what he's doing and does it anyway. 'Gross, jaded adult' is a fun phrase but the scene is primarily serving the emotional plot rather than being a comedy moment.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Two titans clash in the arena of democratic discourse. Magnitude, a force of nature, a hurricane of charisma and pure, distilled school spirit. Leonard, a man who exists primarily in the margins, sustained by nothing but spite and the faint hope that one day, someone will notice him. This election isn't about leadership—it's about the fundamental question: does the universe reward blind optimism, or does it punish those who dare to hope? In the end, we're all voting for the person we wish we were, or running away from the person we fear we've become.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'When we seek to destroy others, we often hurt our self. Because it is the self that wants to be destroyed.' / Jeff: 'Pierce, you're not usually so poignant.' / Pierce: 'Well, Vicki finally lent me her pencil.'
jokes.setup: Pierce delivers an unexpectedly profound observation about self-destruction
jokes.punchline: His wisdom is immediately explained by the pencil loan — Vicki has finally lent him her pencil (the item at the center of earlier conflicts), which apparently unlocked some emotional insight (or more likely is a drug-delivery device)
jokes.explanation: Beautiful three-part structure. The pseudo-profound philosophical observation, the genuine surprise from Jeff ('you're not usually so poignant'), and then the devastating explanation — it was the pencil. The pencil was seeded as a throwaway joke earlier; using it here as the explanation for Pierce's wisdom (or as an implied drug-delivery system) is elegant callback construction. The ambiguity about WHY the pencil made Pierce philosophical is itself funny.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Dude, you're spiraling. You're like a plane that thinks it's too good to land.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: That's not a metaphor, that's just a description of a plane with an existential crisis.

dialogue.speaker: Troy
dialogue.line: Exactly. And we're all on it.

jokes.text: Annie: 'Oh, my God! Pierce! Go to the health center!' — reacting to what Pierce has apparently done with/to the pencil
jokes.setup: Pierce says Vicki lent him her pencil; Annie sees whatever Pierce has done
jokes.punchline: Annie's horrified reaction implies Pierce has done something alarming with the pencil — the joke is entirely in what we DON'T see, only Annie's response
jokes.explanation: Perfect use of the reaction beat. We never see what Pierce did with the pencil — but Annie's 'Go to the health center!' tells us everything we need to know and nothing we want confirmed. The ambiguity (did he snort something? stick it somewhere?) makes it funnier than any explicit answer would be. The callback to the entire pencil thread pays off with maximum dark comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Dean Pelton
dialogue.line: And the winner of this year's election is... the cartoon show!

jokes.text: Abed and Troy's election coverage: 'Two men fighting for the same piece of earth. One recently born. One soon to die. A competition reflecting the pointlessness of life.' / Troy: 'Pull up, Abed. You're in a nosedive.'
jokes.setup: Abed is delivering election coverage commentary on the Magnitude vs. Leonard runoff
jokes.punchline: His commentary spirals from sports-broadcast metaphors into existential nihilism; Troy's interruption — 'Pull up, Abed. You're in a nosedive.' — is delivered as a co-anchor coaching a colleague
jokes.explanation: One of the best exchanges in the episode. Abed's commentary — 'One recently born. One soon to die. A competition reflecting the pointlessness of life' — is a genuinely funny plunge into absurdist philosophy mid-local-news broadcast. Troy's 'Pull up, Abed. You're in a nosedive' is perfect: it uses aviation metaphor to describe Abed's psychological state, delivered with total straight-man sincerity. 'Pull up, you're in a nosedive' is exceptionally quotable.

jokes.text: Dean announces election results: 11 total votes cast. / Crowd: 'Come on, people.'
jokes.setup: Dean announces the final vote tally with gravitas
jokes.punchline: Only 11 people voted at a school with hundreds of students; someone in the crowd calls them out — 'Come on, people'
jokes.explanation: Good beat. The specificity of '11' is funnier than a round number, and the crowd member calling out the low turnout is a nice absurdist touch. Functional gag that serves the larger comedy of the student election satire.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: You know, I've been thinking about my future. I'm gonna run for President.

dialogue.speaker: Garrett
dialogue.line: I'm not gonna win or anything. I just want to be on the ballot so I can tell people I ran for President.

jokes.text: Dean announces: 'The landslide winner of the student election with seven votes is... South Park.'
jokes.setup: The Dean dramatically announces the winner of the election between Magnitude and Leonard
jokes.punchline: In a write-in upset, the Comedy Central cartoon series South Park has been elected president — beating all human candidates with 7 of 11 votes
jokes.explanation: Excellent absurdist punchline to the entire A-plot. South Park winning a student election is exactly the kind of thing Community earns — it's simultaneously a comment on protest votes, the pointlessness of the election, and a funny meta-reference to another irreverent comedy. The Dean's reaction ('Okay. You know what?') followed by his aside that this is exactly what happened ten years ago — implying they've abolished and reinstated student government multiple times over South Park-type results — deepens it perfectly.

dialogue.speaker: Troy (as Kickpuncher)
dialogue.line: Please, just call me Troy.

dialogue.speaker: Villain
dialogue.line: But you're Kickpuncher!

dialogue.speaker: Troy (as Kickpuncher)
dialogue.line: I know, but I'd really prefer Troy. It's my actual name.

jokes.text: Dean: 'I seem to recall this is why we abolished student government in the first place. This is exactly what happened ten years ago.'
jokes.setup: South Park has won the election
jokes.punchline: The Dean reveals this scenario — a protest vote defeating all legitimate candidates — has happened before, implying the entire student government was previously abolished for this exact reason
jokes.explanation: Good institutional-comedy escalation. The implication that Greendale repeatedly abolishes its student government after students elect cartoons or other non-candidates is a great worldbuilding joke. It recontextualizes the entire episode as one node in an absurd recurring cycle.

dialogue.speaker: Abed
dialogue.line: Cool. Cool cool cool cool cool.

jokes.text: Troy: 'Not that shocking to me. I voted for it.' / Abed: 'For real?' / Troy: 'Mm-hmm.' / Abed: 'Me too.' / 'We can never stop being friends.'
jokes.setup: South Park has surprisingly won the election
jokes.punchline: Both Troy and Abed reveal they voted for South Park — and bond over it — 'We can never stop being friends'
jokes.explanation: Perfect Troy and Abed moment. 'We can never stop being friends' as a response to the revelation they both voted for a cartoon is very funny — it treats a trivial shared preference as a profound soul-bond. The escalation from mutual admission to cosmic friendship covenant is very Troy-and-Abed.

jokes.text: Abed's GCTV sign-off: 'Did you know you could make napalm out of common dish soap and cat food?' / Troy: 'What? Why would you say that?'
jokes.setup: Abed signs off his campus news broadcast with a friendly outro
jokes.punchline: Instead of a standard sign-off, he delivers bomb-making instructions — which immediately explains why the Secret Service was surveilling him all episode
jokes.explanation: One of the best structural jokes in the episode. Abed's napalm sign-off retroactively justifies the Secret Service's surveillance of him all episode — they were right to watch him. It's a perfect callback that recontextualizes the entire B-plot: the Secret Service weren't paranoid, Abed IS dangerous. Troy's confused 'Why would you say that?' is the perfect straight-man punctuation. The earned-vs-cheap score is very high because this was planned from the pilot beat — the surveillance setup pays off here.

jokes.text: Vohlers receiving the alert about the elevated threat level, responding 'I'll check it out... personally.' while looking at Abed
jokes.setup: Vohlers is told there's an elevated threat at Greendale and they must move to city college
jokes.punchline: She volunteers to personally investigate — clearly using 'the threat' as her excuse to see Abed again, mirroring Abed's earlier diagnosis of her motivations
jokes.explanation: A satisfying callback payoff to Abed's earlier analysis — she is indeed using a pretext (the elevated threat) to see more of him. The scene structure is clean: Abed predicted this exact behavior and now we watch it happen exactly as he said. Good but mostly reliant on the earlier setup's strength.

jokes.text: Pierce: 'I had a dream I was the regular president.' — delivered directly to camera as a confessional/talking head
jokes.setup: Episode wind-down; Pierce offers his reflection
jokes.punchline: Pierce's dream isn't to be student president — it's to be the ACTUAL president of the United States, and he frames the distinction as 'regular' vs. presumably this lesser version
jokes.explanation: One of the best Pierce lines in the episode. 'The regular president' is perfect — his distinction between the student version and the actual presidency is so understated. He dreamed of the real thing, not this Greendale version. The delivery is entirely matter-of-fact. Near-perfect economy. The word 'regular' is doing all the work.

jokes.text: Troy's Kickpuncher dream sequence: 'You've done so much for our city. Kickpuncher, is there anything we can give you?' / 'Don't call me Kickpuncher. Call me... David.'
jokes.setup: Troy is apparently dreaming alongside Pierce's presidential dream — his dream features Kickpuncher (a recurring fictional action hero from the show's universe)
jokes.punchline: In Troy's dream, Kickpuncher asks to be called 'David' — a mundane name that completely deflates the action-hero mythology
jokes.explanation: Funny juxtaposition of action-hero mythology deflated by the most ordinary name possible. 'Call me David' subverts the superhero naming convention — 'Kickpuncher' wants to be humanized, and 'David' is the least heroic possible name. It works as a coda to the episode's theme of idealism vs. reality.

jokes.text: Abed to Vohlers: 'This was fun. Maybe you can observe me having dinner next time you're in town. Honk twice for yes, once for no.'
jokes.setup: Abed and Vohlers are saying goodbye
jokes.punchline: Abed's date invitation uses car-honking as the RSVP mechanism — framing her response as covert surveillance communication rather than a text or call
jokes.explanation: One of the best lines of the episode. Abed's date proposal is delivered in the language of covert surveillance — 'honk twice for yes, once for no' — which is simultaneously how a spy would communicate AND exactly how Abed would flirt (through the medium of her professional identity). The specificity of 'twice for yes, once for no' is what makes it exceptional. It's romantic, funny, and completely on-brand. Extremely quotable. This is approaching the level of the 'nice soap' joke in terms of originality.

jokes.text: Abed's response to Vohlers leaving: 'Cool. Cool, cool, cool.'
jokes.setup: Vohlers has left; Abed is processing the encounter
jokes.punchline: 'Cool. Cool, cool, cool.' — Abed's signature verbal tic, deployed here to indicate emotional processing he can't otherwise articulate
jokes.explanation: Perhaps the most quotable moment in the episode, though it's less a crafted joke than a character signature. 'Cool cool cool' has become one of Community's most beloved recurring phrases — Abed's way of signaling emotional investment he can't process verbally. Here it ends his only romantic subplot in the episode with perfect understated affect. High quotability and character integration; lower originality because it's a repeated phrase, not a new joke.

tmdb_overview: For an upcoming vice-presidential visit, Glendale's Dean Pelton hastily organizes an election for student body president that pits Annie against Jeff.
insight: Campaign chaos sustains 68 jokes despite middling impact scores across the hour.
